title: Distributed actuators that simultaneously match skeletal muscle

concept.text: The innovation would be a practical artificial muscle that combines useful size, contraction, force, power, efficiency and endurance in one operating device, with the equipment needed to power and control it included in the assessment. The challenge is simultaneous performance: a device that contracts far under a light load, produces high force with little movement, or delivers a brief power burst has not necessarily combined those capabilities in a useful working cycle. Garrad and colleagues describe this integration problem for implantable artificial muscles.

Concept synthesis: extending that goal beyond implants, compact artificial muscles could be placed throughout a machine so that many local actuators coordinate its movement. This would bring actuation closer to the places where force and deformation are needed. Integrating those actuators into load-bearing structures would be a further achievement requiring suitable attachment, structural design and load paths.

significance.text: Conditional engineering significance: combining substantial stroke, useful stress, sustained power and long life in compact units could change how machines are arranged. Powered prostheses, wearables and morphing machines could distribute motion throughout their structures and become less dependent on separate motors and transmissions. The consequential advance would be a useful combination of capabilities at system scale, rather than an isolated record on one actuator metric.

For clinical applications, improved artificial muscles could help restore bodily functions, but actuator performance alone would not establish a usable treatment. Garrad and colleagues identify biomechanical interfaces, encapsulation, energy storage and transmission, and control as necessary supporting capabilities. Their analysis also distinguishes complete replacement of biological muscle from partial augmentation: a device that assists remaining muscle may face different requirements from one expected to supply the entire function.

Interpretive limit: matching selected muscle-like mechanical metrics would not reproduce the full behavior of living muscle or establish general superiority to it. Nor would it by itself demonstrate structural actuation, clinical readiness or widespread adoption. Those outcomes depend on additional integration and application-specific evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is to deliver demanding mechanical performance together, at a useful physical scale and over repeated operation. The supplied article explains that artificial muscles can meet demanding individual targets while still falling short of the combined requirements of the implantable applications it considers. Improving one metric can compromise another, and results at one scale do not automatically transfer to an implantable device. Separate peak values therefore cannot establish the required combination.

A second barrier is integrating the actuator with its supporting systems. Energy storage, energy transmission and control must fit the intended device, while interfaces must transfer mechanical loads and encapsulation must support the intended implantation conditions. An actuator-level result can remain far from a practical implant if the supporting equipment is too burdensome or the interfaces cannot sustain the required operation.

Engineering synthesis: for the broader distributed-actuation concept, the remaining work also includes coordinating multiple units, transferring their forces into the surrounding structure and preserving useful performance after essential supporting mass is counted. Making a structure itself move under load requires demonstrating that its actuator attachments and load paths remain effective throughout deformation and repeated service.

current_state.text: In “Performance metrics for implantable artificial muscles,” Martin Garrad, Ross Burdis, Marcus Drake, Avril D. McCarthy and Jonathan Rossiter conclude that available soft artificial muscles do not meet the combined requirements of the two clinical applications they consider: stress urinary incontinence and sit-to-stand transfer. That conclusion assumes complete replacement of the relevant biological muscle function. It should not be extended automatically to partial assistance, every actuator technology or every nonclinical application.

The article supports the narrower achievement that demanding individual performance targets are attainable, alongside continuing difficulty in combining them. Its prose discusses a target combination of 50–300 mm length, 40% strain, 1.2 MPa stress, at least 60 kJ/m³ work density and 280 W/kg specific power, and separately discusses endurance of approximately one million cycles. These are goals informing the proposed demonstration below; the supplied evidence does not establish that one device has delivered the entire combination, or that ordinary skeletal muscle simultaneously exhibits every listed value.

The research identifies the article as published online on 15 December 2025, with DOI 10.1038/s44222-025-00400-8. The supplied review verified the title, authors and DOI within the retained document, but found a placeholder publication-date field, so that artifact does not confirm the stated date. The source index records retrieval of the accessible PDF on 11 November 2026; retrieval alone does not establish how current the article's assessment remains. The review had no freshness evidence establishing the field's state as of 1 November 2026.

The evidence assessment rests on the article's prose. According to the supplied review, the retained three-page extraction includes the article, references and end matter without truncation, but the figure graphics were not inspected and their extracted numerical layout was ambiguous. The publisher fetch was blocked, while an alternative-host PDF was available. These limitations constrain figure-based comparisons, including claims about exactly which actuators exceed biological muscle; they do not invalidate the prose-supported integration challenge.

completion_criteria.text: Source-grounded target proposal: use a 50–300 mm actuator as the test scale and seek 40% strain, 1.2 MPa stress, at least 60 kJ/m³ delivered work density and 280 W/kg specific power, with endurance of at least 10⁶ cycles. The article supplies the mechanical targets and separately discusses approximately one million cycles. Combining them into one endurance-qualified demonstration is a proposed completion criterion, not a reported achievement or an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: 50–300 mm actuators meet combined mechanical targets for 10⁶ cycles

completion_criteria.text: Proposed system demonstration: operate the device untethered with a documented load and operating cycle, count driver and energy-storage mass in system specific power, and report actuator-only measurements separately. State operating duration, available energy, duty cycle and efficiency so that a brief burst cannot be mistaken for sustained performance. Applying the 280 W/kg threshold to the complete system is an ambitious extension of the source-grounded actuator goal.
completion_criteria.label: Untethered system demonstrates 280 W/kg with full resource accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement requirement: establish stroke, force, delivered work and power consistently from the documented cycle. Peak stress and peak strain need not occur at the same point, so multiplying unrelated maxima would not establish delivered work. Report how work density and specific power are calculated, including volume and mass definitions, and show whether the required performance persists throughout the endurance test. Report degradation, failures and operating conditions alongside successful results.
completion_criteria.label: Cycle-consistent measurements establish delivered performance throughout endurance testing

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirement: demonstrate comparable results across multiple independently fabricated units and provide enough construction and measurement detail for independent replication. To establish distributed actuation, add a structure in which multiple units coordinate useful motion under load; to establish load-bearing structural actuation, demonstrate the relevant attachments and load paths. Define the tested loads, environments and service duration. Finite tests establish performance within those demonstrated boundaries, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independently fabricated units reproduce performance within defined operating boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical boundary: a mechanical demonstration would establish an actuator capability, while claims of useful implantation would additionally require application-specific evidence for interfaces, encapsulation, control, power provision and safe operation. Specify whether the device replaces a muscle function completely or augments remaining function, because those goals impose different demands.
completion_criteria.label: Implantation claims require application-specific evidence and defined functional scope

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MEC-05, “Programmable solids that become different load-bearing mechanisms,” overlaps with distributed actuation when local actuators drive changes in shape or mechanical configuration. MEC-08 concerns the actuator's combined working performance; MEC-05 concerns the solid's ability to become different load-bearing mechanisms. An actuator meeting muscle-like targets would not by itself establish that reconfigurable structural capability.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” and MEC-10, “Stress-directed growth of load-bearing structures,” address distinct structural capabilities that could complement an actuated machine. Long actuator life does not establish fatigue immunity in bulk metals, high actuator stress does not establish near-ideal structural strength, and reversible actuation does not establish stress-directed growth.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-02, “Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts,” MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” and MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” could matter where actuator interfaces, joints or remaining transmissions govern losses and service life. They address friction, life prediction and contact mechanics respectively; meeting MEC-08's actuator targets would not establish those broader capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” could use compact distributed actuators as components, but concerns the broader ability to design practical mechanisms. MEC-14, “Low-cost mechanical storage with high efficiency over long periods,” intersects with the need for energy provision, while addressing storage economics and retention rather than conversion of supplied energy into muscle-like motion. Neither capability follows automatically from MEC-08.

change_log.change: Replaced the broad assertion that artificial muscles exceed biological muscle on individual metrics with the supported statement that demanding individual targets can be met.
change_log.reason: The prose supports individual-target achievement and performance trade-offs; the uninspected, ambiguously extracted figure does not securely establish specific superiority comparisons.

change_log.change: Explained simultaneous performance through a documented working cycle and distinguished actuator performance from complete-system performance.
change_log.reason: Isolated peak values and omitted supporting equipment can obscure whether the proposed capability has actually been demonstrated.

change_log.change: Preserved all numerical completion targets while separating source-grounded targets from proposed untethered operation, system-mass accounting and combined endurance qualification.
change_log.reason: The source grounds the mechanical goals and endurance discussion but does not establish the entire proposed test as achieved or standardized.

change_log.change: Qualified structural actuation and broader machine applications as conditional extensions, and added structural integration and load-path requirements.
change_log.reason: Muscle-like actuator metrics alone do not establish that load-bearing structures can themselves actuate.

change_log.change: Limited the article's unmet-requirements conclusion to its two clinical applications under a complete-replacement assumption.
change_log.reason: Partial augmentation and broader nonclinical uses may impose different requirements.

change_log.change: Integrated clinical interfaces, encapsulation, energy systems and control into the barriers, significance and practical completion boundaries.
change_log.reason: The review identifies these as essential distinctions between an actuator result and a usable clinical system.

change_log.change: Qualified the supplied publication date and retained freshness, publisher-access and figure-extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: The artifact verifies bibliographic identity but not the stated publication date, and the supplied evidence does not establish a current comprehensive field survey.

change_log.change: Added explicitly labeled proposals for reproducibility and distributed structural demonstrations, plus roster-based comparisons.
change_log.reason: These clarify convincing completion and conceptual boundaries without presenting inferred criteria or relationships as source-reported results.

unresolved_issues: The stated online publication date of 15 December 2025 remains unconfirmed because the reviewed artifact contains a placeholder date field.
The supplied evidence does not establish whether later work has changed the article's assessment; the freshness record is empty.
Exact actuator-versus-muscle comparisons that depend on the article's figure remain unresolved because its graphics were not inspected and extracted numerical placement was ambiguous.
The evidence does not establish a device meeting the full proposed target combination. This is a limit of the supplied record, not proof that no such device exists.
The proposed system-level power threshold, endurance qualification and acceptable degradation limits require a fully specified test protocol; they are not established standards.

The target applications and required breadth of structural integration remain open: a successful single actuator, a distributed machine and an implantable clinical device require distinct demonstrations.

brief.title: Artificial muscles that work together inside machines
possible: Powered limbs, wearable supports and machines that change shape could move using compact artificial muscles placed wherever force is needed. Each device would combine strong pulls, substantial shortening and repeated work, with its power supply and controls included.
why: Distributing movement throughout a machine could make its layout less dependent on separate motors and transmissions. Artificial muscles implanted in the body could help people regain bodily functions and maintain mobility and independence.

sources.who: Martin Garrad, Ross Burdis, Marcus Drake, Avril D. McCarthy and Jonathan Rossiter
sources.showed: Their analysis found that soft artificial muscles fall short of the combined demands for fully replacing muscle function in urinary control and rising from a chair. Individual performance targets are attainable.
sources.quote:
soft artificial 
muscles do not yet meet the level of performance required for applica-
tion to SUI or sit-to-stand transfer.
sources.cited_for: Useful artificial muscles must combine mechanical performance with power, control and reliable connections to tissue.
sources.not_established: The analysis does not demonstrate a device meeting all targets together or rule out devices that only assist remaining muscle.

sources.who: E. Acome and colleagues, University of Colorado Boulder
sources.showed: They built soft artificial muscles that use electricity to squeeze liquid. One design lasted over a million cycles under a light load, and stacked devices gripped delicate objects.
sources.quote:
We introduce
prototypical designs of HASEL actuators and demonstrate their robust, muscle-like
performance as well as their ability to repeatedly self-heal after dielectric breakdown —
all using widely available materials and common fabrication techniques.
sources.cited_for: Long endurance and coordinated gripping demonstrate parts of the required capability.
sources.not_established: Endurance under a light load does not establish the full combination of force, shortening and sustained power.

sources.who: Stephan-Daniel Gravert, Elia Varini and colleagues, ETH Zurich
sources.showed: Their HALVE artificial muscles use electricity to squeeze liquid at reduced voltage. They demonstrated a gripper and a robotic swimmer carrying its own power supply.
sources.quote: Last, we demonstrate the utility of HALVE actuators on a robotic gripper and a soft robotic swimmer.
sources.cited_for: Artificial muscles can operate in a moving robot without an external power connection.
sources.not_established: The swimmer does not establish the proposed power target after all supporting equipment is counted, together with long endurance.

sources.who: Amirhossein Kazemipour, Ronan Hinchet and Robert K. Katzschmann, ETH Zurich
sources.showed: A preprint demonstrates paired artificial muscles that pull a joint in opposite directions. Electrically controlled clutches connect and release them, enabling full joint motion without movement lost to loose tendons.
sources.quote:
This configuration
enables an antagonistic joint to achieve a full range of motion
without displacement loss due to tendon slack.
sources.cited_for: Coordinating artificial muscles with clutches can overcome a limitation in joint movement.
sources.not_established: The joint demonstration does not establish the combined performance targets, independent reproduction or lasting structural performance.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated separate pieces: durable artificial muscles, delicate gripping, robots with onboard power and coordinated joint movement. These achievements do not yet establish the full combination in a practical distributed system.
missing: A device still needs to combine useful shortening, force, work, power and endurance at the intended size.
Power storage and controls must fit the device while preserving useful output and efficiency.
Multiple muscles must coordinate movement under load, with attachments that keep transferring force through repeated use.
Implants need reliable tissue connections, protective coverings, control and power provision suited to the bodily function.

milestones.label: Combined performance lasts through repeated use
milestones.explanation: A device at the proposed size would have to meet the contraction, force, work and power targets for a million cycles. This would establish that the capabilities coexist through prolonged use.

milestones.label: The complete system delivers power without external connections
milestones.explanation: The complete system would have to deliver 280 watts per kilogram, counting power electronics and stored energy, with duration and efficiency measured. This would distinguish sustained useful output from a brief burst.

milestones.label: Measurements confirm useful output throughout endurance testing
milestones.explanation: Measurements from the same working cycle would have to establish movement, force, work and power throughout testing, including deterioration and failures. This would prevent unrelated peak values from overstating performance.

milestones.label: Independent devices reproduce performance and coordinate under load
milestones.explanation: Independently made devices would have to reproduce results; distributed and structural claims would need coordinated motion under load and proven force paths. This would establish repeatability and the scope of useful integration.

milestones.label: Implants demonstrate function with suitable supporting systems
milestones.explanation: Implant claims would need evidence for tissue connections, protective coverings, control, power and safe operation, distinguishing assistance from full replacement. This would connect mechanical capability to a defined bodily function.

uncertain: The proposed whole-system power target and endurance requirements are not established standards; acceptable deterioration still needs definition.
The required breadth of demonstration remains open: a single muscle, a distributed machine and a clinical implant establish different capabilities.

page.title: Distributed artificial muscles
page.definition: A machine uses soft actuators, devices that convert energy into deformation, at multiple locations to produce coordinated movement under load. Each actuator meets the published implant-scale muscle-replacement target set; power, control and transmission equipment operate in the tested assembly.

goal.need: An 80 kg person's sit-to-stand movement requires an estimated 400–800 J and 200–800 W. The cited analysis identifies simultaneous actuator performance and support-system integration as requirements for replacing muscle function.

figures.caption: Estimated demands on two muscle functions.
figures.note: Sit-to-stand values cover the gluteus maximus contribution.

statements.context: The FY2025 MURI call, Topic 24, identifies integrated artificial muscle, tendon and skeleton systems as a research objective.

statements.body: University of Colorado Boulder HASEL developers
statements.quote: The performance of natural muscle, in particular mammalian skeletal muscle, is the benchmark for soft actuators
We aim to develop a suitable, compliant artificial muscle system, including the actuator and driving electronics.

completion.title: A powered machine coordinates artificial muscles meeting the combined implant-scale performance targets.
completion.criterion: In one powered machine, artificial muscles at multiple locations coordinate movement under load. Each is 50–300 mm long and reaches at least 40% contraction strain, 1.2 MPa stress, 60 kJ/m³ delivered work density and 280 W/kg peak mechanical specific power in one configuration and loaded operating cycle. Energy supply, drivers, transmission and controls operate in the assembly and enter its total mass and input-energy accounting. The numerical thresholds apply to the actuators.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback combining the published implant-scale target proposal with the distributed-system integration objective.
completion.basis: Searches of ISO/ASTM material, ONR MURI, Army SBIR, CORDIS and performance roadmaps found no adopted combined test for a distributed powered assembly. This fallback joins Garrad et al.'s proposed metrics to ONR's integration goal. The unspecified 280 W/kg target is interpreted as peak power, the narrower requirement; it is not applied to supporting-hardware mass.

milestones.title: A soft actuator converts an applied stimulus directly into mechanical deformation.
milestones.criterion: A compliant actuator directly converts stimulation into contraction, extension or bending. Electrostatic: one donut HASEL actuator sustained >10⁶ cycles lifting 150 g at 15% strain and about 0.75 kPa (5 January 2018). Thermal: one coiled nylon muscle lifted 10 g for 1.2 million cycles at 1 Hz, 30 V/cm and 20% duty cycle (21 February 2014). Fluidic: a type-2 X-PAM lifted 1 kg with 88.1% contraction at 100 kPa (20 September 2023).
milestones.set_by: IEEE Technology Navigator, definition of artificial muscles; a qualitative device-class criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: convert an applied stimulus directly into contraction, extension, or bending in a soft or compliant material

milestones.title: A soft artificial muscle delivers at least 50 W/kg of average mechanical power.
milestones.criterion: Mechanical output divided by contraction time and actuator mass reaches 50 W/kg. Electrostatic: HALVE reached 50.5 W/kg at 1100 V with 300 g (5 January 2024). Thermal: one hydrothermal polyethylene muscle lifted 7.2 kg at 2 Hz, yielding 5.26 kW/kg averaged over the full cycle (21 February 2014). Fluidic: type-3 X-PAM reached 2.3 ± 0.0 kW/kg average at 100 kPa in tests spanning 0.5–3.5 kg loads (20 September 2023). Supply and control mass are excluded. Independent specimen counts are not specified for the HALVE and X-PAM power claims.
milestones.set_by: Mammalian skeletal-muscle comparison convention used by HASEL developers and HALVE researchers. The 50 W/kg average benchmark appears in Table 1 of Rothemund et al.; it is a comparison benchmark, not a certification standard.

milestones.title: Artificial muscles drive a hard skeleton through tough, elastic tendons.
milestones.criterion: Soft artificial muscles transfer force through tough, elastic tendons into hard skeletal load-bearing structures. ONR sets no numerical load or endurance cutoff. Electrostatic evidence: one antagonistic HASEL-clutch joint uses fishing-line tendons and elastic textile sleeves and operates up to 3.2 Hz (3 September 2025 version). Fluidic evidence: one X-PAM elbow flexes >125° and holds 1 kg at 100 kPa (20 September 2023). These demonstrate joint drive; they do not establish the full tendon–skeleton objective.
milestones.set_by: Office of Naval Research, FY2025 MURI funding announcement, Topic 24; a published qualitative integration objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: Another challenge is linking soft muscle-like actuators with tough but elastic tendons, and then binding to hard skeletal load-bearing structures

milestones.title: A 50–300 mm artificial muscle reaches 40% strain, 1.2 MPa, 60 kJ/m³ and 280 W/kg in one cycle.
milestones.criterion: One 50–300 mm soft artificial muscle, in one configuration and loaded operating cycle, reaches at least 40% contraction strain, 1.2 MPa stress, 60 kJ/m³ delivered work density and 280 W/kg peak mechanical specific power. This is the actuator demonstration before distributed integration. Garrad et al. propose the combined metrics without reporting a device that satisfies them. No qualifying joint demonstration was identified for the electrostatic, fluidic or thermal cases.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback based on Garrad et al.'s implantable-muscle proposal. Searches of standards, programmes and performance roadmaps found no adopted protocol for the joint demonstration; the peak-power interpretation is the same as in completion.

not_found: No externally adopted whole-system thresholds for efficiency, endurance, duty cycle or allowable degradation were found.
The implant-scale proposal does not specify an operating waveform or whether its 280 W/kg target is peak or cycle-averaged power.
No published demonstration satisfying the completion test was identified.
No thermal demonstration establishing the stated tendon–skeleton integration objective was identified.
The Garrad publisher page, NASA/JPL arm-wrestling rules and X-PAM supplementary PDF could not be opened.

results.finding: One donut HASEL actuator lifted 150 g for more than 1 million cycles.
results.detail: The actuator operated at 15% strain and approximately 0.75 kPa, with no perceivable loss of performance.
results.quote:
We tested the cycle
life of a donut HASEL actuator used in Fig. 1E for
more than 1 million cycles while lifting 150 g
(actuation stress ~0.75 kPa) at 15% strain and
noticed no perceivable loss of performance (fig. S3).

results.finding: One single-unit HASEL actuator delivered 358 W/kg average specific power during contraction.
results.detail: The actuator operated until mechanical rupture at 158,061 cycles.
results.quote:
Cycle life at high me-
chanical output power was demonstrated with
a single-unit HASEL actuator, which provided
358 W/kg average (586 W/kg peak) specific power
during contraction until mechanical rupture oc-
curred at 158,061 cycles (fig. S12D).

results.finding: Two planar HASEL actuators in parallel powered a robotic arm.
results.detail: The text does not establish force transfer through tough, elastic tendons into a hard skeletal structure.
results.quote:
To demonstrate self-sensing actuation,
we powered a robotic arm with two planar HASEL
actuators combined in parallel and simulta-
neously measured capacitance (Fig. 4, fig. S16,
and movies S7 and S8).

results.finding: One two-unit planar HASEL actuator reached 614 W/kg peak specific power during contraction.
results.detail: The source also reports 124% strain under a 700 g load near resonance, but does not establish the required length, stress and delivered work density together in the specified loaded cycle.
results.quote:
Peak specifi c power during contrac-
tion of the two-unit actuator was 614 W/kg; spe-
cific work during contraction was 70 J/kg (fig. S12)
(24).

results.finding: One HALVE actuator contracted 7% while lifting a load.
results.detail: The actuator lifted 22 g at 800 V.
results.quote:
Figure 3A
shows one of these strain measurements with a HALVE actuator lifting 22 g at 800 V by 7% strain.

results.finding: A HALVE actuator reached 50.5 W/kg average specific power; independent specimen count was not specified.
results.detail: Measured during contraction at 1100 V with a 300 g load; supply and control mass were excluded.
results.quote:
The HALVE actuator reached an average specific power of 50.5 W kg
−1
at an actuation voltage of 1100 V and 75 W kg
−1
at an actuation voltage of 1300 V.

results.finding: One gripper used two HALVE muscle packs to drive jointed fingers through tendons.
results.detail: The gripper transferred force through tendons to its jointed fingers, but tendon toughness and elasticity were not established. A separate elastic element reopened the fingers.
results.quote: Two packs of HALVE muscles are used to generate gripping force. Each pack comprises two individual actuators connected in parallel and composed of three pouches in series. The actuator packs are fixed to the main body at one extremity, while the other extremity is linked to one of the gripping fingers via a tendon.

results.finding: HALVE devices reached 132.7 W/kg peak specific power; independent specimen count was not specified.
results.detail: The reported peak was at 1300 V with a 300 g load, below the 280 W/kg target. The combined strain, stress, work-density and power targets were not demonstrated in one loaded cycle.
results.quote:
The peak specific power in HALVE devices reached 132.7 W kg
−1
at 1300 V for a load of 300 g, which is comparable to mammalian skeletal muscle ranging between 50 W kg
−1
(typical) and 284 W kg
−1

results.finding: One HASEL muscle pack contracted 8% under a 1 N force.
results.detail: The 16 cm pack was operated at 8 kV. The number of independently tested packs is not specified.

results.finding: One antagonistic HASEL-clutch joint operated smoothly up to 3.2 Hz.
results.detail: Fishing-line tendons connected the units to a rigid articulated limb, and elastic textile sleeves assisted motion. The demonstration does not establish the full tough, elastic tendon–skeleton objective.
results.quote:
The coordinated
voltage patterns, up to 3.2 Hz, demonstrate smooth limb
movements without abrupt discontinuities.

results.finding: A 16 cm HASEL muscle pack produced 8% strain under a 1 N force.
results.detail: The reported strain is below 40%; the source does not establish all four required performance thresholds in one loaded cycle. The number of independently tested packs is not specified.

results.finding: Stacked dielectric elastomer actuator, sample size not reported, lifted a 300 g load with 91% linear strain.
results.detail: The source reports more than 100 million actuation cycles for an SBE-based artificial muscle, but does not link that endurance result to the 300 g load test. The tested actuator is not the specified donut HASEL actuator.
results.quote:
A stacked SBE- based artificial muscle with a height of 4.5 mm lifts a 300 g  
(250 times its weight) load by 4.1 mm (91% linear strain).

results.finding: One coiled nylon 6,6 muscle completed 1.2 million actuation cycles.
results.detail: It raised and lowered a 10-g weight at 1 Hz, powered by 30 V/cm at a 20% duty cycle. Creep was below 2%, and stroke amplitude was negligibly affected.
results.quote:
A coiled nylon 6,6 muscle delivered over
1 million cycles during periodic actuation at 1 Hz
(Fig. 3B), raising and lowering a 10-g weight pro-
ducing 22 MPa of nominal stress.

results.detail: The actuator lifted a 1 kg load under 100 kPa of pressure.

results.finding: One wax-filled carbon nanotube yarn muscle delivered 27.9 kW/kg during contraction.
results.detail: The electrothermally powered yarn lifted 175,000 times its mass in 30 ms. High electrical power reduced cycle life through excessive heating and paraffin evaporation.
results.quote:
The work during contraction (0.836 kJ/kg)
provided a power output of 27.9 kW/kg, which is
85 times the peak output of mammalian skeletal
muscles (0.323 kW/kg) ( 23) and 30 times the
maximum measured power density of previous
carbon nanotube muscles.

results.finding: Type 3 X-PAM, independent specimen count not specified: 2.3 ± 0.0 kW/kg average specific power.
results.detail: Dynamic tests used a 100 kPa step pressure and loads spanning 0.5–3.5 kg. Supply and control mass are excluded from the criterion.

−1
